extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of English poetry; literary critics; lecturers; general readers interested in Romantic-era criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extract Hazlitt's evaluative principles for what poetry is, how it should be written and read, and how critics/lecturers should present and judge poets (including portraits of contemporaries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as a natural impression that excites imagination and passion
rubrics_metrics.description: The best general notion of poetry: it is the natural impression of any object or event, by its vividness exciting an involuntary movement of imagination and passion, and producing, by sympathy, a certain modulation of the voice, or sounds, expressing it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hazlitt frames poetry primarily in terms of immediate, involuntary response: vividness that moves imagination and passion and is expressed vocally. He proposes treating poetry by (1) subject-matter, (2) forms of expression, and (3) connection with harmony of sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter must 'come home' — immediate pleasure or pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'relates to whatever gives immediate pleasure or pain to the human mind' and must 'come home to the bosoms and businesses of men'; only what communicates deeply in intelligible shape is fit poetic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjects should be universally intelligible and emotionally resonant (fear, hope, love, hatred, pity, etc.). Hazlitt rejects the idea that poetry is mere ornament or restricted to formal line-lengths; everyday natural phenomena can be poetic in origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is the language of imagination and the passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry represents the world as shaped by imagination and passion rather than as cold, analytic fact; it uses the imagination to mould objects and feelings into heightened forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate poetic language by how well it conveys the interplay of feeling and fancy — whether it 'raises the mind' and expresses the 'excess of the imagination beyond the actual or ordinary impression' of objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of nature mediated by imagination (heightening)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry imitates nature, but the imagination and passions heighten and distort perception; the poet represents objects as they appear under the influence of passion, not as inert fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good poetry does not merely describe natural objects or feelings; it 'heightens' them — e.g., Lachimo's interpretation of the taper near Imogen — and such exaggeration is judged true if it conveys the passionate impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetical impression: an 'uneasy, exquisite sense of beauty or power' impatient of limit
rubrics_metrics.description: A poetical impression is an uneasy, exquisite sense of beauty or power that cannot be contained and strains to link itself to other images of kindred grandeur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess passages by whether they show that restless linking and appetite for amplification — the impulse to enshrine an impression in higher forms of fancy rather than to confine it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of forms and feelings as suggestive and interconnected
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry represents forms chiefly as they suggest other forms, and feelings as they suggest other feelings; it describes flow and motion rather than fixed particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge lines by associative power and capaciousness: does the language evoke a network of related images and emotions rather than isolated description?

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony of sound and modulation of voice as essential forms of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry produces modulation of voice or sounds expressing the impression; its connection with the harmony of sound is a core aspect of poetic form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate attention to rhythm, cadence, and sonic effect: the musical quality should intensify the imaginative impression, not be mere ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparison, contrast, and exaggeration to achieve tragic sublimity or pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poetry reaches sublimity and pathos by comparison and contrast, by exhausting terror or pity through imaginative exaggeration and by bringing all moments of being into startling review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tragic passages by how they escalate feeling (e.g., Lear, Othello): do comparisons and contrasts intensify the emotion, expanding pity or terror rather than restraining it?

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth to nature measured by effected impression under passion, not factual accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic truth is the fidelity of the impression produced under passion; being 'false in point of fact' does not make a passage untrue if it conveys the passionate effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poetic 'truth' by psychological/verbal authenticity (does the line recreate the feeling?) rather than literal factuality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's scope: any human feeling or situation is suitable material
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing that can move the mind — fear, hope, love, hatred, contempt, jealousy, remorse, admiration, wonder, pity, despair, madness — is unfit subject-matter for poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid limiting poetry to narrow topics; evaluate whether a poet treats universal human conditions evocatively and imaginatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's imagination must apprehend more than cooler reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets possess 'seething brains' and 'shaping fantasies' that apprehend beyond what sober reason captures — the poet's eye can 'give to airy nothing a local habitation and a name.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value bold imaginative moves that create new shapes and presences, even if they exceed ordinary rational bounds; judge the quality and control of that imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism should illuminate qualities, not be mechanical or pedantic
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism ought not to tire readers with 'pedantic rules and pragmatical formulas' or the mechanical parts of criticism; it should point out favourite passages, explain objections, and use illustrative remarks without obscuring the poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess critical writing by whether it clarifies, reveals obscured excellences, and uses examples; penalize sterile formalism and trivial critical wrangling that buries poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture technique: read lively extracts, punctuate with lighter matter, and engage the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazlitt's lecturing method: read extracts (even whole narrative poems), punctuate continuous thought with lighter matter, stimulate attention by alternately attracting and repelling, and keep the audience from dozing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For public exposition of poetry, value variety of tone, selection of illustrative passages, rhetorical shocks when appropriate, and an aim to 'share enjoyment' rather than to preach rules. Examples: reading Gay's ribald lines, or entire Tam o' Shanter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraiture/character studies should be linked by a coherent point of view (response to the Spirit of the Age)
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing contemporary portraits, link sketches by a point of view — e.g., the extent of each subject's response to or reaction against the prevailing Spirit of the Age and the era's political/human hopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate biographical or critical portraits by consistency of perspective and by how well each portrait reveals the subject's relation to broader historical movements (Hazlitt's linking device for The Spirit of the Age).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use painterly, vivid word-pictures to render characters and traits
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic/portraitist should use language like a portrait-painter: creating living word-pictures (e.g., Bentham's lack-lustre eye, Moore's mignon figure) that reveal both appearance and inner quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess descriptive criticism by the vividness and aptness of its imagery and whether such images illuminate character or temperament rather than merely caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate artistic admiration from moral/political judgment but include both when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazlitt often dissociates literary admiration from political scorn (e.g., praising Scott's authorship while condemning his political associations), yet he treats moral/political behaviour as relevant to portraiture when it bears on principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating authors, consider artistic merits independently but do not ignore significant moral or political actions that inform a subject's public character; be explicit where the two assessments diverge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harsh criticism may be warranted but should be principled rather than malicious
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazlitt argues that severe portraits (e.g., of Gifford) are not malice if referable to principle; measureless contempt is tolerable when grounded in principled literary or moral objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess critical tone: allow forceful condemnation when substantiated by principle and evidence, but distinguish principled severity from spiteful calumny; include relevant context (e.g., The Beacon affair) to justify intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of lecturing/writing: share genuine enjoyment rather than follow established rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazlitt's aim: to read works with the audience as one would with a friend, point out favourite passages and explain objections, sharing what he enjoyed rather than enforcing pedantic formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate expository writing or lectures by warmth, sincerity, and capacity to communicate delight; penalize performances that prioritize rule-following over communicative pleasure.
